title: How to handle customs and duties for marketplace shipping
body_markdown:
Cross-border orders on Amazon, eBay, Walmart, and Etsy stall at the border more often than sellers admit, and the fix starts with knowing exactly who owes what before the package ships. This guide breaks down how to handle customs duties marketplace shipping without eating margin on returns or losing a buyer to a surprise bill.


**TL;DR**

- Classify every SKU with an HS code before listing internationally — misclassification is the top cause of customs delays in 2026.
- DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) checkout wins for marketplace sellers because it stops surprise fees at the buyer's door.
- US de minimis sits at $800 per shipment in 2026 — price and bundle accordingly to avoid triggering duty.
- SellerChamp centralizes order and inventory data across Amazon, eBay, Walmart, and Etsy so customs paperwork pulls from one accurate source.


## Why this matters

A held package at customs doesn't just delay delivery — it triggers refund requests, negative feedback, and in Amazon's case, account health flags if it happens repeatedly. Buyers on eBay and Etsy who get hit with a surprise duty invoice at the door frequently refuse the package outright, and the seller eats both the original shipping cost and the return freight.

Marketplaces don't standardize customs handling for you. Amazon Global Selling, eBay International Shipping, and Etsy's own carrier programs each have different rules for who collects duty and when. Get this wrong once on a $40 order and it's a rounding error. Get it wrong across 200 international orders a month in 2026 and it's a line item eating your margin.

## What you'll need

- Harmonized System (HS) codes for every SKU you sell internationally
- Country-specific de minimis thresholds for your top 3-5 shipping destinations
- A commercial invoice template with accurate declared values (never zero, never lowballed)
- Carrier accounts or marketplace-managed shipping enrolled in Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) where available
- Centralized inventory and order data — a spreadsheet across five marketplaces will not survive an audit

This is where an [order and inventory system](https://sellerchamp.com/) earns its keep: pulling one accurate SKU record with weight, value, and origin country instead of re-entering data per channel.

## The steps

### 1. Classify every SKU with an accurate HS code

The Harmonized System code determines the duty rate a customs authority applies, and a wrong code either underpays (triggering a hold and back-charge) or overpays (killing your margin for no reason). Look up the 6-digit international code first, then confirm the country-specific extension — the US uses a 10-digit HTS code, the EU uses an 8-10 digit TARIC code.

**Common mistake:** copying a competitor's HS code from a marketplace listing. Codes are seller-declared, not verified by Amazon or eBay, and a wrong code copied from someone else becomes your liability the moment customs opens the box.

### 2. Set declared value to match the actual sale price

Declared value on the commercial invoice must equal what the buyer paid, not a discounted gift value meant to dodge duty. Customs authorities in Canada, the UK, and the EU cross-reference marketplace sale data in 2026 more than they did even two years ago, and a mismatch triggers a manual review that can hold a shipment for 5-10 business days.

This step protects you from the single most common reason for customs holds: undervaluing to help the buyer avoid duty. It backfires almost every time.

### 3. Know the de minimis threshold for each destination

De minimis is the value below which a shipment clears customs duty-free. The US threshold sits at $800 per shipment in 2026, Canada's is roughly CAD 40 for tax and CAD 150 for duty, and the UK's is £135. Price bundles and multi-item orders with these numbers in mind — splitting a $900 order into two $450 shipments can legitimately keep both under a relevant threshold.

**Expected outcome:** fewer shipments cross into duty territory unnecessarily, and the ones that do have an accurate, defensible declared value.

### 4. Choose DDP over DDU for marketplace orders

Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) means you collect and remit duty upfront, so the buyer pays one price at checkout and nothing at the door. Delivered Duty Unpaid (DDU) shifts that surprise bill to the buyer on delivery, and it's the number one reason for refused packages and 1-star reviews on cross-border Etsy and eBay orders.

Amazon Global Selling and eBay International Shipping both support DDP-style programs where the marketplace calculates and collects duty at checkout. Enroll in these before you enroll in the destination country — it removes the collection problem entirely.

### 5. Build customs documentation into your order workflow, not around it

Manually typing commercial invoices per order does not scale past a handful of international orders a week, and it's where HS codes and declared values drift from what's actually accurate. Route every cross-border order through a system that auto-populates invoice data from the same SKU record used for the listing and the inventory count.

This is where inventory-and-order platforms like SellerChamp reduce manual customs paperwork — one product record with HS code, weight, and origin feeds every marketplace instead of five separate manual entries. **Common mistake:** letting each marketplace's shipping label generator populate its own invoice, which creates five slightly different declared values for the same SKU.

### 6. Reconcile duty collected against duty remitted monthly

Marketplaces that collect duty on your behalf (Amazon, in several programs) remit it to customs authorities, but you're still responsible for confirming it matches what was actually owed. Run a monthly reconciliation between duty collected at checkout and duty paperwork filed by the carrier.

**Why it matters:** a gap here either means you're overpaying (money you can recover) or underpaying (a liability that compounds with more orders). Catching this quarterly instead of monthly in 2026 means a small gap becomes a large one.

### 7. Flag high-duty categories before you list them internationally

Textiles, electronics, and certain home goods carry higher duty rates in most destination countries than the average seller expects — sometimes 15-25% versus a flat 5-8% baseline. Check the duty rate for your specific HS code and destination before you turn on international shipping for that SKU, not after the first held shipment.

**Expected outcome:** you avoid listing a $30 item that costs $9 in duty to deliver, which kills the unit economics before the first sale ships.

## Troubleshooting

- **Package held at customs with no explanation.** Check the HS code against the destination country's tariff schedule first — a mismatched code is the most common trigger, and correcting it with a customs broker usually clears the hold within days.
- **Buyer refuses delivery over a duty invoice.** Switch that lane to DDP immediately; a refused DDU package costs you the outbound freight, the return freight, and the refund.
- **Duty charged twice on the same order.** This happens when both the marketplace's DDP program and the destination carrier apply duty separately — audit which programs are actually enrolled per marketplace, not assumed.
- **Declared value disputed by customs.** Keep the original sale receipt or order confirmation on file; a documented sale price beats a customs officer's estimate every time.
- **Repeated holds on one specific SKU.** The HS code is almost certainly wrong for that product category — reclassify it and update every marketplace listing at once, not just the one that got flagged.
- **Duty remittance doesn't match marketplace reports.** Pull the reconciliation report monthly rather than quarterly in 2026 — a three-month gap is much harder to trace back to a specific order batch.

## Tools and resources

- HS/HTS code lookup tools published by your destination country's customs authority (US ITC, UK Trade Tariff, EU TARIC)
- Marketplace-specific DDP enrollment pages (Amazon Global Selling, eBay International Shipping)
- A customs broker for any category with duty rates above 15%, especially textiles and electronics
- [SellerChamp](https://sellerchamp.com/) for centralizing SKU data, inventory counts, and order routing across Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy so customs paperwork stays consistent everywhere it's generated

## What to do next

Audit your top 10 international SKUs this week: confirm the HS code, confirm the declared value matches actual sale price, and confirm which marketplace program is handling duty collection. That single pass catches most of the errors that cause held shipments in 2026.

## FAQ


**How do I handle customs duties for marketplace shipping in 2026?**

Classify each SKU with an accurate HS code, declare the real sale value, and enroll in Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) programs where the marketplace offers them so the buyer pays duty upfront instead of at delivery. This removes most customs holds and refused packages.

**What is the US de minimis threshold for customs duty?**

The US de minimis threshold is $800 per shipment in 2026, meaning orders valued at or below that amount typically clear without duty. Other countries have much lower thresholds, so check each destination separately.

**Is DDP or DDU better for cross-border ecommerce orders?**

DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) is better for marketplace sellers because it collects duty at checkout instead of surprising the buyer at delivery. DDU shipments have a much higher rate of refused packages and negative reviews.

**What happens if an HS code is wrong on an international shipment?**

An incorrect HS code triggers a customs hold for manual review, which can delay delivery by 5-10 business days and sometimes results in a back-charge for underpaid duty. Reclassifying the SKU correctly across every marketplace listing prevents repeat holds.

**Who collects customs duty on Amazon and eBay international orders?**

Amazon Global Selling and eBay International Shipping both offer programs that collect duty at checkout and remit it to the destination country, but sellers should still reconcile collected duty against filed paperwork monthly to catch mismatches.

**How much does customs duty typically cost on ecommerce shipments?**

Duty rates vary by category and destination, with textiles and electronics often running 15-25% while many general goods sit at 5-8%. Checking the rate for your specific HS code before listing internationally avoids unprofitable SKUs.

**Can declaring a lower value avoid customs duty?**

No — declared value must match the actual sale price, and customs authorities increasingly cross-reference marketplace sale data in 2026. Underdeclaring triggers manual review holds far more often than it saves in duty.

**How often should I reconcile duty collected versus duty remitted?**

Reconcile monthly rather than quarterly, since a small gap between collected and remitted duty is far easier to trace back to a specific order batch within 30 days than after three months.


## One last thing

The sellers who avoid customs headaches in 2026 aren't the ones with the best broker relationship — they're the ones whose SKU data (HS code, weight, declared value, origin) is identical across every marketplace it touches. Fix the data once at the source and the paperwork downstream stops drifting.
